summary: This RFC defines an RTP payload format for streaming video encoded as JPEG 2000 codestreams, with sub-codestream latency: the first packet for an image can be sent before the sender has the whole image.

plainLanguage.summary: A picture can be sent in pieces while still being drawn. Viewers see it sooner.

questions: what is rtp payload format for jpeg 2000
what is a resync point in jpeg 2000 rtp
what is the media type for jpeg 2000 over rtp
subtitle: How to stream JPEG 2000 video over RTP so packets can leave before the whole frame is encoded.

tldr.problem: Existing ways of sending JPEG 2000 video over RTP rely on codestream structures that can only be written after the whole image is encoded, which adds delay for live production.
tldr.mechanism: The payload format splits each codestream into Main Packets and Body Packets with small payload headers that mark resync points, resolution levels and quality layers, so the first packet of an image can be sent early and packets can be dropped or recovered without parsing the codestream.
tldr.outcome: Senders get sub-codestream latency, and receivers or intermediate systems can discard resolution levels or quality layers by reading only packet headers. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9828 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2025. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a New JPEG 2000 Payload Format
sections.content:
RFC 9828 defines how a video signal encoded as a sequence of JPEG 2000 codestreams is carried in the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP, RFC 3550). RTP moves real-time data but leaves the payload to companion payload format documents. The RFC lists target uses such as real-time TV production over IP, remote presence and surveillance.

The headline feature is sub-codestream latency: the first RTP packet of a codestream can be emitted before the whole codestream is available. That rules out the PLM and PLT marker segments for recovery after packet loss, because those can only be written once the codestream is complete. The RFC contrasts this with RFC 5371, which also carries JPEG 2000 but relies on structures that need the complete codestream.

The format also borrows an extended sequence number from RFC 4175, offers an optional finer-grained timestamp offset, and adds code-block caching for screen content, progressive segmented frame support and explicit colorspace signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Older methods waited for the whole picture before sending anything. This one starts sending right away, so the person watching sees it sooner.

sections.title: A Primer on JPEG 2000 Codestreams
sections.content:
A JPEG 2000 image is one or more components (for example Y, C_b and C_r) on a common grid, optionally cut into independently coded tiles. Each image is a standalone codestream: marker segments carrying coding parameters, plus coded data. It starts with an SOC marker segment and ends with an EOC marker segment, and the main header sits between SOC and the first SOT.

A wavelet transform splits the image into resolution levels, each with half the horizontal and vertical resolution of the next. The coded data is made of code-blocks, grouped into precincts. The order these appear in the codestream is the progression order, built from Position (P), Component (C), Resolution level (R) and Quality layer (L). The RFC notes that PRCL is particularly useful for subframe latency operation.

The payload format supports three ways of scanning frames: progressive, interlaced (two fields) and progressive segmented frame (two segments, one of odd lines and one of even lines).
sections.plainLanguage: A JPEG 2000 picture is stored like a stack of layers, from a small blurry version up to the full sharp one. The order the layers are written in decides what the viewer sees first.

sections.title: Main Packets and Body Packets
sections.content:
Every RTP packet is either a Main Packet or a Body Packet. Each is the RTP fixed header, a payload header, and a fragment of a JPEG 2000 codestream. A fragment need not hold complete JPEG 2000 packets. Successive codestreams may be separated by padding bytes, which the sender MUST set to zero and the receiver MUST ignore.

The RFC defines an Extended Header as the bytes from the SOC marker up to and including the first SOD marker. A Body Packet MUST NOT contain any of it, a Main Packet MUST contain at least one byte of it, and no payload may mix bytes from more than one codestream.

In the RTP fixed header, the marker bit is 1 when the payload contains an EOC marker. The timestamp is the presentation time of the image, uses a 90 kHz clock, and is equal for all packets of one image. For interlaced frames, Field 2 is offset from Field 1 by half the frame period. The 16-bit sequence number is extended: the ESEQ field times 65536, plus the RTP sequence number. The RFC gives an example where the plain sequence number rolls over in 0.5 seconds on a 1 Gbps stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The first box of a delivery has the instruction sheet for the whole picture. The later boxes just have more pieces. Every box carries a number so you can tell if one went missing.

sections.title: The Payload Headers
sections.content:
The Main Packet payload header starts with MH (2 bits), which says whether the packet is a Main Packet and whether more follow, and TP (3 bits), the image type (progressive, one of the interlaced fields, or one of the PsF segments). ORDH (3 bits) gives the progression order for the whole codestream and whether resync points are signaled. It MUST be 0 for multi-tile codestreams, and only ORDH values 4 (PCRL) and 6 (PRCL) allow sub-codestream latency.

Other fields include P and PTSTAMP (12 bits, an optional fine timestamp), ESEQ (8 bits), R (header reuse across codestreams), S and PRIMS, TRANS, MAT, RANGE (explicit colorimetry using ITU-T H.273 code points, with component layouts such as Y, RGB or YCbCr, optionally with an opacity channel), C (code-block caching) and XTRAC/XTRAB (extension space).

The Body Packet header repeats MH, TP, PTSTAMP and ESEQ and adds RES (3 bits), ORDB (1 bit), QUAL (3 bits), POS (12 bits) and PID (20 bits). PID is c + s * num_components, identifying the precinct of a resync point, and a payload with a PID MUST NOT contain bytes from more than one precinct.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box has a small label. The first box's label describes the whole picture, such as its colors. Later labels say how sharp this piece is and where it fits.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
A sender emits either one Main Packet with MH = 3, or one or more with MH = 1 followed by one with MH = 2. Main Packet header fields MUST be identical across a codestream except MH, ESEQ and PTSTAMP. A sender SHOULD set P = 1 only if it can generate PTSTAMP accurately, and SHOULD set RES above 0 whenever possible. It MUST set XTRAC and unassigned values to 0 and MUST NOT use extension values.

A resync point is the first byte of JPEG 2000 packet header data for a precinct. A receiver can use one to keep decoding after earlier packets were corrupted, lost or deliberately discarded. It plays a role similar to pointer marker segments, but for high-bandwidth, low-latency streaming.

Because RES and QUAL sit in the packet header, an intermediate system MAY strip packets a client does not need, and a receiver can discard packets where QUAL is above some N to keep only quality layers N and below. Dropping Body Packets where RES is greater than N reduces the maximum decodable resolution by a factor of 2^(7 - N) when all wavelet stages are horizontal and vertical.

Receivers MUST accept non-zero XTRAC and ignore XTRAB, MUST ignore unassigned values, and MUST discard packets with an extension value.

With code-block caching (C = 1), a sender can send static parts of the video only occasionally and send empty code-blocks otherwise. The receiver replaces an empty code-block from its cache and updates the cache when a non-empty one arrives. R MUST be 1 when C is 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Because every box says how detailed it is, a helper along the way can throw away the extra-detailed boxes if the road is crowded. You still get a smaller picture, just not as sharp.

sections.title: Media Type and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The payload format is registered as media type video/jpeg2000-scl. Optional parameters are pixel, sample, width, height, signal, caps and cache. For pixel, sample and signal, a relative reference must match a format defined in the RFC's appendices, such as rgb444sdr or ycbcr422pq (pixel), samples of 8, 10, 12 or 16 bits (sample) and prog, psf, tff or bff (signal). cache must be true for C to be 1.

Mapping to the Session Description Protocol follows RFC 4855. There is no single congestion control scheme for all uses. The RFC lists examples: offering several streams at different data rates, changing resolution, frame rate or compression ratio, or having an intermediate system discard resolution levels or quality layers. RTCP feedback can help with rate adaptation.
sections.plainLanguage: The format has a name tag so programs can recognise it, and a few settings that say what kind of picture to expect. If the road gets crowded, you can send smaller or blurrier pictures.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and any RTP profile in use. As the RFC notes, it is not the payload format's job to mandate how confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity are achieved. Applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong security mechanisms.

The RFC says the format and its decoder show no significant non-uniformity in receiver-side computational complexity, so they are unlikely to pose a denial-of-service threat from pathological data, and that the format has no active content. The media type registration warns that JPEG 2000 memory needs vary greatly with image size (width and height up to 2^32 - 1 pixels), so implementations SHOULD take care and fail gracefully when resource limits are exceeded.
sections.plainLanguage: The format does not lock the box itself, so you should use a lock from elsewhere. Also, a huge picture needs a lot of space, so your computer should say no politely when it runs out.

fields.name: TP
fields.desc: Image type: progressive, field or segment.

fields.name: XTRAC
fields.desc: Length of XTRAB in multiples of 4 bytes.

fields.name: ESEQ
fields.desc: High-order bits of the extended sequence number.

fields.name: RES
fields.desc: Resolution level the payload contributes to.

fields.name: QUAL
fields.desc: Lowest quality layer the payload contributes to.

fields.name: ESEQ
fields.desc: High-order bits of the extended sequence number.

fields.name: POS
fields.desc: Byte offset of the resync point in the payload.

fields.name: PID
fields.desc: Precinct identifier of the resync point.

items.label: Main Packet, more follow
items.desc: More than one Main Packet; the next packet is a Main Packet.

items.label: Last Main Packet
items.desc: More than one Main Packet; the next packet is a Body Packet.

items.label: Only Main Packet
items.desc: Exactly one Main Packet in the codestream.
